analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give cash refunds for canceled or badly delayed flights and refundable cancellations.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on February 28, 2023 and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required large airlines and ticket sellers to offer travelers a full cash refund — including fees — within 30 days when a flight is canceled or significantly delayed, or when the passenger cancels their ticket at least 48 hours before departure. Airlines could still offer vouchers, but the vouchers would have to last forever and come with a clear notice that the passenger can demand cash instead. Passengers who took vouchers during the COVID-19 shutdowns could have swapped them for cash, and airlines would have had to disclose the refund right before selling a ticket. The bill never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers — especially families and workers buying nonrefundable tickets — would gain a guaranteed way to get their money back in cash when plans fall through or airlines cancel flights, instead of being steered toward vouchers or expiring credits. Passengers who accepted vouchers during the pandemic would be able to convert them to cash.

how_it_helps.text: Requires major airlines to offer a full cash refund — including fees — within 30 days of a request when a flight is canceled or significantly delayed.
Gives travelers the right to cancel their own ticket at least 48 hours before departure and get their money back in cash, not just a voucher.
Bans expiring vouchers: any credit or voucher an airline offers must stay valid indefinitely and must clearly tell the passenger they can demand cash instead.
Lets passengers who accepted vouchers during the COVID shutdowns (from March 2020 onward) still swap them for cash refunds, and lets refund-providing travel agents get reimbursed by the airlines.
Requires airlines to tell buyers before purchase that they can cancel for a full cash refund, and sets a $1,000 civil penalty per violation.

analysis.who_pays: Major airlines (those with over $1.5 billion in 2018 revenue) and ticket agents would bear refund costs, disclosure requirements, and $1,000 civil penalties per violation. Travelers who might otherwise accept cheaper restricted fares could face somewhat higher ticket prices as carriers price in the refund obligation.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the definition of a "significantly delayed" flight up to the Secretary of Transportation, so the scope of the refund guarantee depends entirely on how future administrations define that term.

The refund right for passenger-initiated cancellations applies only when a ticket is canceled at least 48 hours before departure, so last-minute changes — a common traveler situation — would not qualify.

The bill would impose new refund, disclosure, and reporting costs on airlines and ticket agents, which carriers would argue raise administrative expenses, and the bill restricts which federal COVID-era funds airlines could use to pay refunds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to travelers — guaranteed cash back when a flight is canceled or a trip is called off — are concrete and low-risk to the broader economy; the costs to airlines are real but limited to cases where they already failed to deliver the service sold. The main design concern is that "significantly delayed" is left to the Transportation Secretary to define, leaving room for industry-friendly interpretation, and the 48-hour advance-cancellation right is narrower than full refundable flexibility.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ed Markey introduced the bill on February 28, 2023 with seven Democratic and independent cosponsors including Sanders, Warren, and Blumenthal.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major airlines kept their existing practices: vouchers instead of cash, credits that can expire, and no general refund for passenger-initiated cancellations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines, who avoided mandatory cash refunds

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring cash refunds for canceled or significantly delayed flights and for passenger cancellations made 48 hours ahead.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Sanders, Schatz, Warren, Whitehouse, and Wyden, and Rep.-turned-Sen. Peter Welch (original cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction (7 Democrats and 1 independent).

against.name: Major passenger airlines and their trade group Airlines for America
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory cash refunds and expiring-voucher bans as Congress and the Transportation Department weighed refund rules; the industry generally prefers credits over cash obligations. No airline opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All eight Senate supporters were Democrats or an independent aligned with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past a Democratic-run committee referral.

industries.industry: Major passenger airlines (carriers with over $1.5 billion in 2018 revenue)
industries.note: The bill forces large carriers to return ticket money in cash when flights are canceled or significantly delayed, to honor indefinitely valid vouchers, to allow 48-hour-advance cancellations, and to pay $1,000 civil penalties per violation. Airlines have historically preferred vouchers and credits because many go unused or expire.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and ticket agents
industries.note: Agents would have to process refunds and disclose the refund right to buyers, but the bill guarantees they get promptly reimbursed by the airlines for the ticket price they pass back.
